slides.narration: Every phone, laptop and solar panel depends on semiconductors such as silicon. On their own they conduct electricity only slightly, but adding a tiny amount of the right impurity changes them dramatically. In this part we use the idea of energy bands to see why some solids conduct and others do not, and how doping makes n-type and p-type semiconductors.

slides.heading: From energy levels to energy bands
slides.body_md: In an isolated atom electrons have sharp energy levels. In a crystal, the atoms are so close that each level **spreads into a band** of very closely spaced levels.
bullets: **Valence band:** the band holding the valence electrons (full at 0 K in a semiconductor).
**Conduction band:** the next band up; electrons here are free to move and carry current.
**Band gap** $E_g$: the forbidden energy range between them.

slides.narration: An isolated atom has neat, separate energy levels. Bring about ten to the twenty eight atoms together in a cubic metre of crystal and their outer levels overlap and split into bands of extremely closely spaced levels. The valence band holds the bonding electrons. Above it, after a forbidden gap, is the conduction band, where electrons can move freely. The size of that gap decides everything.

slides.heading: Conductors, semiconductors and insulators
slides.body_md: Compare the band gaps:
bullets: **Conductors:** bands overlap, so many electrons are free.
**Semiconductors:** a small gap; at room temperature a few electrons gain enough thermal energy to cross it.
**Insulators:** a large gap; practically no electrons cross it.

visual.alt: Table comparing conductors, semiconductors and insulators: band gap, typical resistivity and effect of temperature

slides.narration: In a metal the valence and conduction bands overlap, so there are always plenty of free electrons: a good conductor. In an insulator like diamond the gap is over five electronvolts, far more than thermal energy at room temperature, which is only about point zero two five electronvolt, so it hardly conducts. Silicon, with a gap of about one electronvolt, lies in between: a semiconductor.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: light across the gap
slides.body_md: Find the longest wavelength of light that can lift an electron across the band gap of (a) silicon (1.1 eV), (b) germanium (0.7 eV), (c) diamond (5.4 eV). (Use $hc = 1243$ eV nm.)
bullets: (a) $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E_g} = \dfrac{1243}{1.1} \approx 1130$ nm (infrared): all visible light can create electron–hole pairs in Si.
(c) $\dfrac{1243}{5.4} \approx 230$ nm (ultraviolet): visible light cannot, which is why diamond is transparent.

slides.narration: A photon can lift an electron across the gap only if its energy is at least the gap energy. For silicon that means wavelengths shorter than about eleven hundred nanometres, which includes all visible light: that is why silicon solar cells work. For diamond the limit is about two hundred and thirty nanometres, in the ultraviolet, so visible light passes straight through.

slides.heading: Intrinsic semiconductors: electrons and holes
slides.body_md: A pure (**intrinsic**) semiconductor such as Si or Ge: each atom forms four covalent bonds.
bullets: Thermal energy breaks a few bonds: an electron goes to the conduction band and leaves a **hole** (a missing electron) that acts as a **positive** charge carrier.
In an intrinsic semiconductor $n_e = n_h = n_i$.
Holes "move" as neighbouring electrons jump into them; in a field, electrons and holes drift in opposite directions but both contribute to current: $I = I_e + I_h$.
At 0 K an intrinsic semiconductor is an insulator; its conductivity rises with temperature.

slides.narration: In pure silicon every atom shares its four outer electrons with four neighbours. At room temperature, thermal vibrations break a few of these bonds. Each freed electron leaves behind a hole, a gap in a bond, which behaves like a positive charge. Nearby electrons can hop into the hole, so the hole moves. In pure silicon the numbers of free electrons and holes are equal.

slides.heading: Doping: n-type
slides.body_md: Add a tiny amount (about 1 in 10⁶) of a **pentavalent** impurity (P, As, Sb):
bullets: Four of its five valence electrons form bonds; the **fifth** is very loosely bound (about 0.01–0.05 eV) and is easily freed.
The impurity **donates** an electron: a **donor**. Electrons become the **majority** carriers, holes the minority.
The donor ion left behind is **positive** but fixed; the crystal as a whole stays **neutral**.

slides.narration: Replace one silicon atom in a million with arsenic, which has five outer electrons. Four of them form bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms, and the fifth is left hanging, so loosely held that room temperature frees it. Arsenic donates electrons, so it is called a donor. Now there are far more free electrons than holes: an n-type semiconductor, n for negative carriers.

slides.heading: Doping: p-type
slides.body_md: Add a **trivalent** impurity (B, Al, In):
bullets: It forms only three bonds; the fourth bond lacks an electron, leaving a **hole**.
A neighbouring electron can fill it, so the impurity **accepts** an electron: an **acceptor**. Holes become the **majority** carriers.
The acceptor ion becomes **negative** but fixed; the crystal stays neutral.

slides.narration: Now replace a silicon atom with boron, which has only three outer electrons. One of its four bonds is missing an electron: a hole. An electron from a nearby bond easily drops into it, so boron accepts electrons and is called an acceptor. The holes it creates outnumber the free electrons, so this is a p-type semiconductor, p for positive carriers.

slides.heading: n-type and p-type compared
slides.body_md: In any doped semiconductor in equilibrium, $n_e n_h = n_i^2$.

visual.alt: Table comparing n-type and p-type semiconductors: dopant valency, donor or acceptor, majority and minority carriers, and overall neutrality

slides.narration: Here is the comparison. Pentavalent donors make n-type material, with electrons as majority carriers; trivalent acceptors make p-type material, with holes as majority carriers. Both remain electrically neutral overall, because every free carrier is balanced by a fixed ion. Increasing one kind of carrier reduces the other, because the product of the electron and hole densities stays equal to n i squared.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: carriers in n-type silicon
slides.body_md: Pure silicon has $5 \times 10^{28}$ atoms m$^{-3}$ and $n_i = 1.5 \times 10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$. It is doped with 1 arsenic atom per $10^{6}$ silicon atoms. Find the electron and hole densities.
bullets: Step 1 — $N_D = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{28}}{10^{6}} = 5.0 \times 10^{22}$ m$^{-3}$; each donor gives one electron, so $n_e \approx 5.0 \times 10^{22}$ m$^{-3}$ (thermal electrons are negligible).
Meaning — doping raises the electron density over a million times and reduces the holes enormously.

visual.alt: Table comparing n-type and p-type semiconductors: dopant valency, donor or acceptor, majority and minority carriers, and overall neutrality

slides.narration: One arsenic atom per million silicon atoms gives five times ten to the twenty two donors per cubic metre, each supplying an electron, millions of times more than the thermally produced carriers. The holes do not stay at their intrinsic value: the product rule gives only about four point five times ten to the nine per cubic metre. A tiny impurity changes the material completely.

slides.heading: Temperature and conduction
slides.body_md: Why heating affects metals and semiconductors oppositely:
columns:
**Metal**
- Number of free electrons fixed
- Heating increases collisions
- Resistance rises

**Semiconductor**
- Heating frees many more carriers
- This outweighs extra collisions
- Resistance falls

visual.alt: Table comparing conductors, semiconductors and insulators: band gap, typical resistivity and effect of temperature

slides.narration: Heat a copper wire and its resistance goes up, because its fixed supply of free electrons collides more often with vibrating ions. Heat a semiconductor and its resistance goes down, because thermal energy frees many more electrons and holes across the small band gap, and this effect is much bigger than the increase in collisions. This is the basis of thermistors.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Valence band, band gap, conduction band
Overlap: conductor; gap ≈ 1 eV: semiconductor; > 3 eV: insulator
n_e = n_h = n_i; holes are positive carriers
$n_e n_h = n_i^2$; doped crystal still neutral

visual.alt: Summary table of energy bands, classification of solids, intrinsic semiconductors, n-type and p-type doping and the product rule

slides.narration: To sum up: in a solid, energy levels spread into bands. Overlapping bands make a conductor, a small gap a semiconductor and a large gap an insulator. Pure semiconductors have equal numbers of electrons and holes. Pentavalent donors make n-type material with electrons in the majority, trivalent acceptors make p-type material with holes in the majority, and the crystal stays neutral throughout.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Draw three band diagrams side by side, labelling the valence band, conduction band and $E_g$.
Name the dopants: P, As, Sb (donors, n-type); B, Al, In (acceptors, p-type).
Say that doped semiconductors are electrically **neutral**.
Use $n_e n_h = n_i^2$ for minority-carrier problems.

rows: Vacancy of an electron in a bond; acts as +e
Why resistance of Si falls on heating?

visual.alt: Table of common questions and the key point for each

slides.narration: Band diagrams are easy marks if they are labelled clearly. Learn which elements are donors and which are acceptors by their valency, five or three. A common trap: n-type material is not negatively charged; it is neutral, because every free electron is matched by a fixed positive ion. And for carrier numbers, use the product rule.

slides.narration: Put a piece of p-type silicon in contact with a piece of n-type silicon and something remarkable happens at the boundary: the junction lets current through easily in one direction but hardly at all in the other. This device, the junction diode, is in every phone charger. In this part we see how the junction forms, how it behaves, and how diodes turn alternating current into direct current.

slides.heading: Formation of the depletion layer
slides.body_md: At the junction, electrons **diffuse** from n to p and holes from p to n, where they recombine.
bullets: This leaves a thin **depletion layer** with no mobile carriers, containing fixed **negative acceptor ions** (p side) and **positive donor ions** (n side).
These ions set up an **electric field from n to p** and a **barrier potential** (about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge) that opposes further diffusion.
Equilibrium: **diffusion current** (majority carriers) = **drift current** (minority carriers pushed by the field).

slides.heading: Forward and reverse bias
slides.body_md: Connect a battery across the junction:
bullets: **Forward bias** (p to +, n to −): the applied voltage **opposes** the barrier; the depletion layer **narrows**; majority carriers cross and a **large** current (mA) flows once V exceeds about 0.7 V (Si).
**Reverse bias** (p to −, n to +): the barrier **increases** and the layer **widens**; only a tiny **minority-carrier** current (μA) flows, almost independent of voltage, until **breakdown**.

slides.narration: In forward bias the positive terminal is joined to the p side. The applied voltage works against the barrier, the depletion layer shrinks, and once about point seven volt is reached, majority carriers flood across: a large current. In reverse bias the battery adds to the barrier, the depletion layer widens, and only the few minority carriers drift across, giving a tiny current, until at a high enough voltage the junction breaks down.

slides.heading: Forward characteristic
slides.body_md: Current rises very slowly at first, then **sharply** beyond the **knee (threshold) voltage**, about 0.7 V for Si and 0.3 V for Ge.
bullets: The I–V graph is **not** a straight line: a diode is a **non-ohmic** device.
Dynamic resistance $r_d = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I}$ is small above the knee.

visual.alt: Forward characteristic of a silicon diode: almost no current until about 0.6 volts, then the current rises very steeply beyond the knee voltage of about 0.7 volts
visual.caption: Below the knee the barrier blocks most carriers; above it the current rises exponentially.

slides.narration: Here is the forward characteristic of a silicon diode, drawn from a simple model. Below about point six volt almost nothing flows. Around point seven volt, the knee, the current shoots up, multiplying several times for every extra tenth of a volt. The graph is a curve, not a straight line, so the diode does not obey Ohm’s law. Its dynamic resistance, delta V over delta I, is only a few ohms above the knee.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: dynamic resistance
slides.body_md: From the forward characteristic, the current is 10 mA at 0.70 V and 33.2 mA at 0.76 V. Find the dynamic resistance in this range.
bullets: Step 2 — $r_d = \dfrac{\Delta V}{\Delta I} = \dfrac{0.06}{0.0232} \approx 2.59$ Ω.

visual.alt: Forward characteristic of a silicon diode: almost no current until about 0.6 volts, then the current rises very steeply beyond the knee voltage of about 0.7 volts
visual.caption: Below the knee the barrier blocks most carriers; above it the current rises exponentially.

slides.narration: Read two points on the steep part of the curve. A rise of six hundredths of a volt raises the current from ten to about thirty three milliamperes. Dividing, the dynamic resistance is about two and a half ohms. In the reverse direction, by contrast, a whole volt changes the current by almost nothing, so the reverse resistance is enormous: that is what makes the diode a one-way valve.

slides.heading: Reverse characteristic
slides.body_md: In reverse bias the current is tiny (μA for Si) and almost constant — the **reverse saturation current** — because it depends only on the number of minority carriers.
bullets: At the **breakdown voltage** the reverse current rises sharply.
Ordinary rectifier diodes are operated well below breakdown.

visual.alt: Reverse characteristic of a diode: a tiny, nearly constant reverse current of about one microampere until the breakdown voltage, where the current increases sharply
visual.caption: Note the different scale: microamperes in reverse, milliamperes forward.

slides.narration: In reverse bias, only minority carriers can cross, and there are very few of them, so the current is a microampere or less and hardly changes with voltage: it is the reverse saturation current. At a large enough reverse voltage, the breakdown voltage, the current suddenly increases. Rectifier diodes are chosen so that this never happens in normal use.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a diode in a circuit
slides.body_md: A silicon diode (0.7 V drop when conducting) is connected in forward bias in series with a 1.0 kΩ resistor across a 5.0 V battery. Find the current. What is the current if the diode is reversed?
bullets: Step 1 — voltage across the resistor $= 5.0 - 0.7 = 4.3$ V.
Reversed — the diode blocks: only the reverse saturation current (about a microampere or less) flows.

slides.heading: Half-wave rectifier
slides.body_md: A diode in series with a load across the secondary of a transformer:
bullets: When end A is **positive**, the diode is forward biased and current flows through the load.
In the other half-cycle it is reverse biased: **no current**.
Output: pulses of one direction (pulsating DC) at the **same frequency** as the input.

visual.alt: Half-wave rectification: the input is a sine wave; the output follows only the positive half-cycles and is zero during the negative half-cycles
visual.caption: Output pulses at the input frequency; half the input is wasted.

slides.narration: In a half-wave rectifier, a single diode connects the transformer to the load. During one half of each cycle the diode is forward biased and current flows; during the other half it is reverse biased and blocks. The load receives a series of positive humps with gaps in between, one hump per cycle, so the output frequency equals the mains frequency. Half the input is wasted.

slides.heading: Full-wave rectifier
slides.body_md: Two diodes and a **centre-tapped** transformer:
bullets: When A is +, **D₁** conducts; when B is +, **D₂** conducts.
In both half-cycles current flows through the load in the **same direction**.

slides.narration: A full-wave rectifier uses a transformer whose secondary has a centre tap, and two diodes. In one half-cycle end A is positive and diode one conducts; in the next, end B is positive and diode two conducts. Either way, current goes through the load in the same direction. The output has a hump in every half-cycle, so its pulse frequency is twice that of the input.

slides.heading: Waveforms compared
slides.body_md: Input and output voltages:
bullets: Half-wave: one pulse per cycle (output frequency $f$).
Full-wave: two pulses per cycle (output frequency $2f$), smoother and more efficient.
A **capacitor filter** across the load smooths the pulses into nearly steady DC.

slides.narration: Compare the outputs. The full-wave output fills in the gaps left by the half-wave rectifier, with a hump every half-cycle. That makes it easier to smooth: a large capacitor across the load charges up at each peak and then supplies current in between, giving an almost steady direct voltage, like the output of a phone charger.

sections.heading: 1. Energy bands
sections.body_md:
- In a crystal, atomic energy levels spread into **bands**: the **valence band** (valence electrons) and the **conduction band** (free electrons), separated by the **band gap** $E_g$.
- **Conductor:** bands overlap; many free electrons; resistivity about $10^{-8}$–$10^{-6}$ Ω m.
- **Semiconductor:** small gap, about 1 eV (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV); a few electrons cross it at room temperature; resistivity about $10^{-5}$–$10^{6}$ Ω m; resistance **falls** on heating.
- **Insulator:** large gap, over 3 eV (diamond 5.4 eV); resistivity about $10^{11}$–$10^{19}$ Ω m.
- A photon can create an electron–hole pair only if $h\nu \ge E_g$, i.e. $\lambda \le hc/E_g$.

sections.heading: 2. Intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors
sections.body_md:
- **Intrinsic** (pure Si, Ge): thermal energy breaks bonds, creating equal numbers of free electrons and **holes**: $n_e = n_h = n_i$. A hole is a missing electron in a bond and behaves as a **positive** carrier. Current $I = I_e + I_h$.
- **n-type:** doped with a **pentavalent** impurity (P, As, Sb), a **donor**; majority carriers **electrons**, minority holes.
- **p-type:** doped with a **trivalent** impurity (B, Al, In), an **acceptor**; majority carriers **holes**, minority electrons.
- Doping level is tiny (≈ 1 in 10⁶) but raises conductivity enormously. Doped crystals remain electrically **neutral** (fixed ions balance the carriers).
- In equilibrium $n_e n_h = n_i^2$.

key_terms.definition_md: A vacancy left by an electron in a covalent bond; it acts as a positive charge carrier.
A pentavalent impurity atom that gives a free electron.
A trivalent impurity atom that creates a hole.

sections.heading: 3. The p-n junction and its characteristics
sections.body_md:
- **Formation:** electrons diffuse from n to p and holes from p to n and recombine, leaving a **depletion layer** of fixed ions (negative on the p side, positive on the n side). The field points **n → p**, creating a **barrier potential** (≈ 0.7 V Si, ≈ 0.3 V Ge). In equilibrium, diffusion current = drift current.
- **Forward bias** (p to +): barrier lowered, depletion layer **narrows**; current rises sharply above the **knee voltage**; current in mA.
- **Reverse bias** (p to −): barrier raised, depletion layer **widens**; tiny, nearly constant **reverse saturation current** of minority carriers (μA); sharp rise at the **breakdown voltage**.
- The diode is **non-ohmic**; dynamic resistance $r_d = \Delta V/\Delta I$.

sections.heading: 4. The diode as a rectifier
sections.body_md:
- **Rectification:** converting AC into unidirectional (DC) current, using the diode’s one-way conduction.
- **Half-wave:** one diode in series with the load; conducts only in half-cycles when it is forward biased; output frequency = input frequency $f$.
- **Full-wave (centre tap):** two diodes; D₁ conducts when one end of the secondary is positive, D₂ in the other half-cycle; current through the load is always in the same direction; output pulse frequency $2f$.
- Peak output ≈ peak input − diode drop (≈ 0.7 V for Si); $V_0 = \sqrt{2}V_\text{rms}$.
- A **capacitor filter** across the load smooths the pulsating output.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about band gaps is correct?

options.text_md: Conductors have the largest band gap
Insulators have the largest band gap and conductors have none (their bands overlap)
Semiconductors have a larger band gap than insulators
All three have the same band gap but different numbers of electrons

questions.solution_md: Conductor: bands overlap; semiconductor: about 1 eV; insulator: more than about 3 eV — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a solid, the energy band in which electrons are free to move through the crystal and carry current is called the ___ band.
questions.solution_md: The **conduction** band.

questions.stem_md: A piece of pure germanium is warmed from 20 °C to 60 °C. Its electrical resistance

options.text_md: decreases, because more electrons are excited across the band gap
increases, because the atoms vibrate more
stays the same, because germanium is pure
becomes zero

questions.solution_md: In a semiconductor the number of carriers rises steeply with temperature, outweighing the extra collisions — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Gallium arsenide has a band gap of 1.42 eV. Find the longest wavelength of light that can create an electron–hole pair in it, in nm (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $\lambda_\text{max} = \dfrac{hc}{E_g} = \dfrac{1243}{1.42} \approx 875$ nm (near infrared).

questions.stem_md: A photodetector made of a certain semiconductor responds to light of wavelengths up to 1.65 μm but not beyond. Estimate its band gap, in eV (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $E_g = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_\text{max}} = \dfrac{1243}{1650} \approx 0.753$ eV.

marking_scheme.step: E_g = hc/λ_max with λ in nm

questions.stem_md: True or false? In an insulator, the valence band and the conduction band overlap.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Overlapping bands are characteristic of conductors; insulators have a large band gap (over about 3 eV).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between conductors, semiconductors and insulators on the basis of energy bands.

answer.model_answer_md: In **conductors** the valence and conduction bands **overlap**, so many electrons are free to conduct. In **semiconductors** a **small** band gap (about 1 eV) separates them, so a few electrons cross at room temperature. In **insulators** the gap is **large** (over about 3 eV), so practically no electrons reach the conduction band.

questions.solution_md: Overlap, small gap, large gap.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Diamond is transparent to visible light.

**Reason (R):** The band gap of diamond (about 5.4 eV) is larger than the energy of any visible photon (at most about 3.1 eV).

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: visible photons cannot lift electrons across the gap, so they are not absorbed — option (a).

questions.stem_md: For a solar cell that must absorb most of the visible spectrum (400–700 nm), which of these materials is most suitable?

options.text_md: Diamond (band gap 5.4 eV)
Zinc sulphide (band gap 3.6 eV)
Copper (no band gap)
Silicon (band gap 1.1 eV)

questions.solution_md: Visible photons have 1.8–3.1 eV, more than 1.1 eV, so silicon absorbs them all; diamond and ZnS gaps are too large, and copper cannot separate charges — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Why does the resistance of a semiconductor decrease on heating, while that of a metal increases?

answer.model_answer_md: In a **metal** the number of free electrons is **fixed**; heating makes the ions vibrate more, increasing **collisions**, so resistance **rises**. In a **semiconductor**, heating excites **many more** electrons across the small band gap (creating electrons and holes); this large rise in the **number of carriers** outweighs the extra collisions, so resistance **falls**.

questions.solution_md: Collisions vs carrier number.

marking_scheme.step: Semiconductor: many more carriers outweigh collisions

questions.stem_md: Pure germanium is doped with a small amount of indium (a group 13, trivalent element). The result is

options.text_md: an n-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
a p-type semiconductor with holes as majority carriers
a p-type semiconductor with electrons as majority carriers
an intrinsic semiconductor

questions.solution_md: A trivalent acceptor leaves a hole in a bond: p-type, holes in the majority — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An n-type semiconductor is electrically neutral.

**Reason (R):** The extra free electrons in it are balanced by an equal number of fixed positive donor ions.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true, and R explains A: each donor that gives up an electron becomes a fixed positive ion — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The vacancy left in a covalent bond when an electron is freed, which behaves as a positive charge carrier, is called a ___.
questions.solution_md: A **hole**.

questions.stem_md: A pentavalent impurity such as phosphorus added to silicon is called

options.text_md: an acceptor, because it accepts an electron
a donor, because it supplies a free electron
a donor, because it supplies a hole
an acceptor, because it supplies a free electron

questions.solution_md: Its fifth valence electron is almost free, so it donates an electron — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Silicon (nᵢ = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³) is doped with 1.0 × 10²¹ acceptor atoms per m³. Find the density of electrons, in units of 10¹¹ m⁻³ (3 significant figures).

In a doped semiconductor at room temperature, the electron density is 5.0 × 10²⁰ m⁻³ and the hole density is 8.0 × 10¹¹ m⁻³. Find the intrinsic carrier density, in units of 10¹⁶ m⁻³. Is the material n-type or p-type?
questions.solution_md: $n_i = \sqrt{n_e n_h} = \sqrt{5.0 \times 10^{20} \times 8.0 \times 10^{11}} = \sqrt{4.0 \times 10^{32}} = 2.0 \times 10^{16}$ m$^{-3}$, i.e. $\dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{16}}{10^{16}} = 2.0$. Electrons are the majority: n-type.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the depletion layer and the barrier potential are formed at a p-n junction.

answer.model_answer_md: Electrons are the majority on the n-side and holes on the p-side, so electrons **diffuse** into the p-side and holes into the n-side, where they **recombine**. This leaves a thin region near the junction with **no mobile carriers** but with fixed **negative** acceptor ions on the p-side and **positive** donor ions on the n-side: the **depletion layer**. These ions create an electric field from n to p and a **potential barrier** that opposes further diffusion; equilibrium is reached when the **drift** of minority carriers balances the **diffusion**.

questions.solution_md: Opposes vs adds to the junction field.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain how energy bands are formed in a solid. (b) With band diagrams (described in words), distinguish between conductors, semiconductors and insulators. (c) The band gaps of silicon and diamond are 1.1 eV and 5.4 eV. Find the longest wavelength each can absorb by exciting electrons across the gap, and use your answers to explain why diamond is transparent while silicon is opaque to visible light. (hc = 1243 eV nm.)

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) In an isolated atom electrons occupy sharp energy levels. In a crystal, about $10^{28}$ atoms per m³ are so close that their outer levels interact and split into very many closely spaced levels: **bands**. The valence electrons fill the **valence band**; the next band is the **conduction band**; between them is the **band gap**.

(b) Conductor: bands overlap. Semiconductor: small gap (≈ 1 eV), so a few electrons are excited at room temperature. Insulator: large gap (> 3 eV), practically no electrons in the conduction band.

(c) Si: $\lambda_\text{max} = \dfrac{1243}{1.1} \approx 1130$ nm; diamond: $\dfrac{1243}{5.4} \approx 230$ nm. Visible light (400–700 nm) has wavelengths shorter than 1130 nm, so silicon absorbs it (opaque); but longer than 230 nm, so diamond cannot absorb it (transparent).

questions.solution_md: Bands from interacting levels; three diagrams; λ = hc/E_g.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A forward-biased silicon diode conducts appreciably only when the applied voltage exceeds about 0.7 V.

**Reason (R):** Forward bias makes the depletion layer of the diode wider.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true: the applied voltage must overcome the barrier potential. R is false: forward bias NARROWS the depletion layer — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Germanium has a band gap of 0.70 eV. Find the longest wavelength of light that can create an electron–hole pair in germanium, in nm (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $\lambda_\text{max} = \dfrac{hc}{E_g} = \dfrac{1243}{0.70} \approx 1780$ nm (infrared).

questions.stem_md: A red light-emitting diode gives out light of wavelength 650 nm when electrons fall across its band gap. Estimate the band gap of its semiconductor, in eV (3 significant figures). (hc = 1243 eV nm.)
questions.solution_md: $E_g \approx \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1243}{650} \approx 1.91$ eV.

questions.stem_md: Germanium has 4.4 × 10²⁸ atoms m⁻³ and an intrinsic carrier density of 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³. It is doped with 1 arsenic atom per 10⁶ germanium atoms. Find the hole density, in units of 10¹⁶ m⁻³ (3 significant figures).
A silicon diode (0.7 V drop when conducting) is to carry a forward current of 15 mA from a 9.0 V battery. What series resistance is needed, in ohms (3 significant figures)?
A filament lamp is run from the AC mains, first directly and then with a silicon diode in series. With the diode in place the lamp

options.text_md: glows less brightly, because current flows only in alternate half-cycles
does not glow at all, because a diode blocks AC
glows more brightly, because the diode adds energy
glows equally brightly, because the diode has no resistance

questions.solution_md: The diode conducts only in the half-cycles when it is forward biased, so the lamp receives about half the power — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a centre-tap full-wave rectifier, each half of the secondary gives 6.0 V rms. With silicon diodes (0.7 V drop), find the peak voltage across the load, in volts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $V_0 = \sqrt{2} \times 6.0 \approx 8.49$ V; peak across the load $= 8.49 - 0.7 = 7.79$ V.

questions.stem_md: A silicon diode is reverse biased in series with a 1 kΩ resistor across a 5.0 V battery (well below breakdown). The voltage across the diode is about

options.text_md: 0.7 V, the barrier potential
0 V, because the diode blocks
5.0 V, because almost no current flows, so almost no voltage is lost across the resistor
2.5 V, shared equally with the resistor

questions.solution_md: The reverse current is only microamperes, so the resistor drop (IR) is negligible and nearly the whole 5.0 V appears across the diode — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Near its knee, the forward current of a silicon diode follows I = I₁ e^((V − 0.70 V)/0.050 V), where I₁ is the current at 0.70 V. By what factor does the current increase when the voltage rises from 0.70 V to 0.80 V (3 significant figures)?
A full-wave rectifier is fed from 50 Hz mains. Find the time between successive output pulses, in milliseconds.
questions.solution_md: Output pulse frequency $= 2 \times 50 = 100$ Hz, so the interval $= \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.010$ s, i.e. $0.010 \times 10^{3} = 10$ ms.

questions.stem_md: The donor concentration in a piece of n-type silicon is doubled (it is still much larger than nᵢ). The hole density

options.text_md: is halved
is doubled
is unchanged
becomes four times as large

questions.solution_md: n_e roughly doubles and n_e n_h = n_i² stays fixed, so n_h halves — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each silicon sample in Column A with the description of its charge carriers in Column B.

options.text_md: Silicon doped with phosphorus
Silicon doped with boron
Pure silicon at room temperature
Pure silicon near 0 K

match_right.text_md: Equal numbers of free electrons and holes

questions.solution_md: Phosphorus (donor) → electrons in the majority (1 → q); boron (acceptor) → holes in the majority (2 → s); pure Si at room temperature → equal numbers (3 → p); pure Si near 0 K → no free carriers (4 → r).
